In dup_mmap()
column2: using __mt_dup() to duplicate the old maple tree and then

column1: directly replacing the entries of VMAs in the new maple tree can result in
better performance.  __mt_dup() uses DFS pre-order to duplicate the maple
tree
The average time complexity of __mt_dup() is O(n)
of VMAs.  The proof of the time complexity is provided in the commit log
that introduces __mt_dup().  After duplicating the maple tree
element is traversed and replaced (ignoring the cases of deletion
are rare).  Since it is only a replacement operation for each element
this process is also O(n).
Analyzing the exact time complexity of the previous algorithm is
challenging because each insertion can involve appending to a node
pushing data to adjacent nodes
column2: or even splitting nodes.  The frequency of

column1: each action is difficult to calculate.  The worst-case scenario for a
single insertion is when the tree undergoes splitting at every level.  If
we consider each insertion as the worst-case scenario
that the upper bound of the time complexity is O(n*log(n))
is a loose upper bound.  However
the actual time complexity is likely to be O(n).
As the entire maple tree is duplicated using __mt_dup()
fails
column2: there will be a portion of VMAs that have not been duplicated in

column1: the maple tree.  To handle this
column2: we mark the failure point with

column1: XA_ZERO_ENTRY.  In exit_mmap()
releasing VMAs that have not been duplicated after this point.
